about: Sourced life stories for the kings of Assyria (Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sargon, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon) and of Babylon (Merodach-baladan, Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-merodach, Belshazzar). Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossier Research/People/rulers-assyria-babylon.md.

tiglath-pileser-2ki-15-19.short: Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria took Galilee, Gilead and Naphtali in Pekah's days, and answered Ahaz's appeal by taking Damascus and slaying Rezin.

paragraphs.text: Scripture gives this king of Assyria no father, no length of reign and no account of his death; it knows him only through his dealings with Israel and Judah. Kings spells his name Tiglath-pileser, and Chronicles Tilgath-pilneser. “In the days of Pekah king of Israel” he came and took Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee and “all the land of Naphtali”, and carried the people captive to Assyria.

Kings also tells of “Pul the king of Assyria”, who came against the land in the reign of Menahem king of Israel; Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, raised at fifty shekels from each of the mighty men of wealth, and the king of Assyria turned back. Chronicles says that the God of Israel “stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria”, and that “he carried them away”: the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh, to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan. Beerah, prince of the Reubenites, was one whom Tilgath-pilneser carried away. Scripture does not say whether Pul and Tiglath-pileser are one king.

When Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel besieged Ahaz in Jerusalem, Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser: “I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me”. With them he sent the silver and gold found in the house of the LORD and in the treasures of the king's house. Kings says “the king of Assyria hearkened unto him”, went up against Damascus and took it, carried its people captive to Kir, and slew Rezin.

King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser, saw an altar there, and sent its pattern to Urijah the priest, who built one like it in Jerusalem. Ahaz also turned the covert for the sabbath and the king's entry from the house of the LORD “for the king of Assyria”. Chronicles tells the alliance otherwise: Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria for help, and “Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria came unto him, and distressed him, but strengthened him not”; though Ahaz gave him a portion out of the house of the LORD, the king's house and the princes', “he helped him not”.

That is all Scripture tells of him. The next king of Assyria that Kings names is Shalmaneser, who came up against Hoshea king of Israel. Whether Pul is this king, and what his own records say, are set out on his page as a ruler.

shalmaneser-2ki-17-3.short: Shalmaneser king of Assyria made Hoshea of Israel his servant, and came up against Samaria and besieged it; at the end of three years it was taken.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Shalmaneser king of Assyria in two places in Kings, and gives him no father, no length of reign and no account of his death. “Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria”, Kings says of Hoshea king of Israel, “and Hoshea became his servant, and gave him presents.”

Then the king of Assyria found conspiracy in Hoshea, who had sent messengers to So king of Egypt and brought no present to the king of Assyria, “as he had done year by year”. So “the king of Assyria shut him up, and bound him in prison”. These verses call him only “the king of Assyria”.

Kings dates the siege to the fourth year of Hezekiah king of Judah, the seventh of Hoshea: “Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria, and besieged it.” “At the end of three years they took it”, in Hezekiah's sixth year and Hoshea's ninth, and the king of Assyria carried Israel away to Halah, to Habor by the river of Gozan, and to the cities of the Medes. Kings does not name the king who took the city: one account says “the king of Assyria took Samaria”, the other “they took it”. It gives the reason: “they obeyed not the voice of the LORD their God, but transgressed his covenant”.

Hosea warned Israel that its fortresses would be spoiled “as Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel in the day of battle”. Hosea does not say who Shalman was. Whether he is this king, and which king of Assyria took Samaria, are set out on his page as a ruler.

sargon-isa-20-1.short: Sargon king of Assyria is named once in Scripture, as the king who sent his Tartan against Ashdod in the year Isaiah walked naked and barefoot.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Sargon only once. Isaiah dates a word of the LORD “In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it”. That is all it says of what Sargon did.

At that time the LORD told Isaiah the son of Amoz to loose the sackcloth from his loins and put off his shoe, and he did so, “walking naked and barefoot”. He walked so three years, as a sign upon Egypt and Ethiopia: “So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives”. Those who had looked to Ethiopia and Egypt for help would say, “how shall we escape?”

Isaiah does not name the king of Assyria in the sign, and Scripture tells nothing else of Sargon: not his family, his reign or his death. Who he was, and what his own records say, are set out on his page as a ruler.

sennacherib-2ki-18-13.short: Sennacherib king of Assyria came against Judah's fenced cities in Hezekiah's fourteenth year and threatened Jerusalem; he went home to Nineveh, and two of his sons killed him.

paragraphs.text: Scripture does not name Sennacherib's father. Kings and Isaiah say that “in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah” he came up against all the fenced cities of Judah “and took them”. Chronicles says he entered Judah and encamped against the fenced cities, “and thought to win them for himself”; it does not say he took them.

Kings tells that Hezekiah sent to him at Lachish, “I have offended; return from me”, and that the king of Assyria appointed him three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. Hezekiah gave him all the silver found in the house of the LORD and in the king's treasures, and cut off the gold from the doors of the temple. Chronicles does not mention this tribute.

Then the king of Assyria sent Tartan, Rabsaris and Rab-shakeh from Lachish with a great host against Jerusalem; Chronicles says he himself laid siege against Lachish, “and all his power with him”. By the conduit of the upper pool Rab-shakeh cried to the people on the wall in the Jews' language, mocked their trust in Egypt and in the LORD, and asked, “Hath any of the gods of the nations delivered at all his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?” Rab-shakeh went back and found him warring against Libnah; hearing that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia had come out to fight him, he sent messengers again to Hezekiah: “Let not thy God in whom thou trustest deceive thee”. Chronicles says he wrote “letters to rail on the LORD God of Israel”.

Hezekiah spread the letter before the LORD and prayed. Isaiah sent him word that the LORD had heard his prayer “against Sennacherib king of Assyria”, and that the LORD said to the king: “I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest.” Kings and Isaiah say that the angel of the LORD smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and eighty-five thousand; Chronicles says an angel “cut off all the mighty men of valour, and the leaders and captains”, and gives no number. “So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh”; Chronicles says “he returned with shame of face to his own land”.

Isaiah had said the LORD would cause him “to fall by the sword in his own land”. Kings and Isaiah say that as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword and escaped into the land of Armenia, and Esar-haddon his son reigned in his place. Chronicles says that when he came into the house of his god, “they that came forth of his own bowels slew him there with the sword”; it names no son. Scripture does not say where that house stood, or how long after his return he died; his reign and his own annals are set out on his page as a ruler.

esarhaddon-2ki-19-37.short: Esar-haddon, Sennacherib's son, reigned in his father's place; in Zerubbabel's day the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin said he had brought them there.

paragraphs.text: Esar-haddon was a son of Sennacherib king of Assyria. When two other sons, Adrammelech and Sharezer, smote their father with the sword as he worshipped in the house of Nisroch his god, and escaped into the land of Armenia, “Esar-haddon his son reigned in his stead”. Isaiah tells it in the same words.

Scripture names him once more. When the children of the captivity were building the temple, the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin came to Zerubbabel asking to build with them: “we seek your God, as ye do; and we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esar-haddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither.” Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the chief of the fathers answered, “Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God”.

Scripture records no campaign of his against Israel or Judah, gives no length for his reign, and does not say how he died. Chronicles tells that “the captains of the host of the king of Assyria” took Manasseh king of Judah and carried him in fetters to Babylon, but it does not name the king. Which king that was, and what Esar-haddon's own records say, are set out on his page as a ruler.

merodach-baladan-2ki-20-12.short: Merodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah after his sickness, and Hezekiah showed his envoys all his treasures.

paragraphs.text: Isaiah calls him “Merodach-baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon”; Kings spells the name “Berodach-baladan”. Scripture gives no length for his reign and names no other member of his family. He appears in one story, told in both books.

Kings says he sent letters and a present to Hezekiah, “for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick”; Isaiah says he had heard “that he had been sick, and was recovered”. Kings says Hezekiah “hearkened unto them”, Isaiah that he “was glad of them”, and he showed the envoys the house of his precious things, the silver, the gold, the spices and the ointment, and all the house of his armour: “there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not”.

Isaiah the prophet asked Hezekiah where the men had come from, and he answered, “from a far country, even from Babylon”. Isaiah then gave the word of the LORD: all that was in Hezekiah's house “shall be carried into Babylon”, and some of his sons would be eunuchs “in the palace of the king of Babylon”.

Chronicles speaks instead of “the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon, who sent unto him to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land”, and says that in this business God left Hezekiah “to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart”. Scripture says nothing more of Merodach-baladan. When he reigned, and his wars with Assyria as other records tell them, are set out on his page as a ruler.

nebuchadnezzar-2ki-24-1.short: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took Jerusalem and carried Judah captive; Daniel tells of his dreams, his golden image, his humbling, and his praise of the King of heaven.

paragraphs.text: Kings, Chronicles and Daniel spell his name Nebuchadnezzar; Ezekiel, and Jeremiah mostly, spell it Nebuchadrezzar. Scripture does not name his father. Jeremiah calls the fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah “the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon”, and says that in that year he smote the army of Pharaoh-necho by the river Euphrates in Carchemish. Through Jeremiah the LORD calls him “Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant”.

Kings says Jehoiakim became his servant three years and then rebelled, and that Jehoiakim “slept with his fathers”; Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound him in fetters to carry him to Babylon. Daniel dates a siege of Jerusalem to Jehoiakim's third year, when the king carried part of the vessels of the house of God to the house of his god, and had young men of Israel, of the king's seed and of the princes, taught the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans. Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah were among them.

In the eighth year of his reign Jehoiachin king of Judah went out to him and was taken. He carried away the treasures of the house of the LORD, ten thousand captives and all the craftsmen and smiths, and made Mattaniah king in Jehoiachin's place, changing his name to Zedekiah. Chronicles says Zedekiah rebelled against the king “who had made him swear by God”. Nebuchadnezzar came with all his host against Jerusalem; Zedekiah was brought to him at Riblah, where his sons were slain before his eyes, and in Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year Nebuzar-adan, captain of the guard, burned the house of the LORD and all the houses of Jerusalem.

He gave charge concerning Jeremiah to Nebuzar-adan: “Take him, and look well to him, and do him no harm”. Over the people left in Judah he made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam ruler. Ezekiel says he “caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus”, “yet had he no wages”, and that the LORD would give him the land of Egypt for it. His reign, year by year, is told on his page as a ruler.

Daniel tells of him in Babylon. In the second year of his reign he dreamed, and when the wise men could not tell him the dream, he commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed. Daniel told him the dream, a great image broken by a stone “cut out without hands”, and said to him, “Thou art this head of gold.” The king fell upon his face and worshipped Daniel, said “your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings”, and made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon.

He set up an image of gold, threescore cubits high, in the plain of Dura. When Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego would not worship it, he had them bound and cast into the burning fiery furnace, heated seven times more than it was wont; then he saw four men loose, walking in the fire, and called the three out unhurt. He blessed their God and decreed that none should speak amiss against him, “because there is no other God that can deliver after this sort”.

In a letter to all peoples he told of a second dream, of a great tree hewn down, which Daniel said was the king himself. At the end of twelve months, as he walked in his palace and said, “Is not this great Babylon, that I have built”, a voice from heaven said the kingdom was departed from him; he was driven from men and ate grass as oxen, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers. At the end of the days his understanding returned and he was established in his kingdom again, and he wrote: “Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven”. Scripture does not say how long he reigned or how he died.

evil-merodach-2ki-25-27.short: Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year he began to reign, brought Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison and gave him a place at his table.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Evil-merodach in two places that tell one story, and does not name his father or say how long he reigned. Kings says that “in the year that he began to reign” he lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison, in the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month. Jeremiah says “in the first year of his reign”, on the twenty-fifth day of that month.

He spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon. Jehoiachin changed his prison garments and ate bread before him continually, with an allowance from the king, “a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life”. Jeremiah says the same, adding “until the day of his death”.
Scripture does not say why he released Jehoiachin, whose son he was, or how his reign ended. Those questions, and what other records say of him, are set out on his page as a ruler.

belshazzar-dan-5-1.short: Belshazzar, king of Babylon as Daniel calls him, saw a hand write on his palace wall during a feast; Daniel read it, and that night he was slain.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Belshazzar only in Daniel, which calls him “Belshazzar the king” and dates two of Daniel's visions by his years: a dream “In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon”, and a vision “In the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar”. Daniel 5 calls Nebuchadnezzar his father: the queen speaks of “the king Nebuchadnezzar thy father”.

He made a great feast to a thousand of his lords and, as he tasted the wine, commanded that the gold and silver vessels taken out of the temple at Jerusalem be brought, so that he, his princes, his wives and his concubines might drink from them. They drank wine and “praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone”. In the same hour the fingers of a man's hand wrote upon the plaister of the palace wall; the king's countenance was changed, his knees smote one against another, and his wise men could not read the writing.

The queen came into the banquet house and told him of Daniel, whom Nebuchadnezzar had made master of the magicians. Daniel told the king to keep his gifts, reminded him how Nebuchadnezzar had been driven from men when his heart was lifted up, and said, “thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this”. He read the writing, MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN: God had numbered the kingdom and finished it; “Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting”; the kingdom was divided, and “given to the Medes and Persians”.

Belshazzar commanded, and they clothed Daniel with scarlet, put a chain of gold about his neck, and proclaimed him “the third ruler in the kingdom”. “In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain. And Darius the Median took the kingdom”. Scripture does not say who killed him or how. What other records say of his family and his kingship is set out on his page as a ruler.
